location.region: Wuyishan (also Anxi and other Fujian regions as a foundational cultivar)

characteristics.cultivar: Shui Xian (one of Fujian's oldest and most widespread cultivars)

description.short: Full-bodied, woody Wuyi rock oolong, serving as one of the foundational and most classic pillars of Yancha
description.overview: Shui Xian is not just a specific tea but also one of southern China's most celebrated legacy cultivars, anchoring the Wuyi rock tea tradition alongside Rou Gui. Tea harvested from old bushes (Lao Cong) yields an exceptionally deep, mossy, and woody complexity.
description.leaf: Large, bold, dark-brown twisted leaves with slight oily sheen
description.liquor: Rich amber-orange to deep brownish infusion
description.aroma: Woody and nutty with dry floral nuances and pronounced mineral character
description.taste: Mellow, full-bodied, slightly sweet, rich in woodiness and smoothed by rocky minerality (yan yun)
description.processing: Plucking → withering → tossing/bruising (yao qing) → fixation (kill-green) → strip rolling → prolonged traditional charcoal roasting

history.origin: According to legend, the parent bush was discovered growing wild beside a rocky cave pool ('shui' meaning water, 'xian' meaning immortal or nymph) in northern Fujian.
history.development: The Shui Xian cultivar spread widely beyond Wuyishan, becoming a cornerstone variety cultivated across Fujian and northern Guangdong for dark and medium oolongs.
history.modern: Old-bush harvests (Lao Cong Shui Xian) from trees aged 60 to over 100 years are prized by connoisseurs worldwide for their distinctive mossy, woody, and mineral depth.
interestingFacts: Shui Xian is one of the rare versatile cultivars crafted into heavily roasted Wuyi rock oolongs, roasted Guangdong Dancongs, and lighter Minnan styles.
Although the Chinese characters '水仙' are also the name for the narcissus/daffodil flower, the tea's character is grounded in rich wood and minerals rather than perfumed floral sweetness.
